drafts.angle: SCOREBOARD: «Humans vs Rabbits» told as five rounds, with a running score that only appears on screen (a toon outback cricket scoreboard). Each round is one human weapon and how the rabbits answered it. R1 the fence: the rabbits got there first and were even scratching to get back (Rabbits 1). R2 the £25,000 prize: Pasteur enters with chicken cholera, nobody wins (Rabbits 2). R3 myxoma 1950: mosquitoes spread it and it kills 99 % of infected rabbits (Humans 1). R4 the rabbits evolve (Rabbits 3). R5 calicivirus breaks out of its island quarantine, probably on flies, and works before the official release (Humans 2, «if you count the flies»). It ends on the final score «so far», which leaves the match open, and a callback: the fence's second career keeping out emus, with «Good luck with that» winking at the emus without stating anything about them.

drafts.angle: C: «Famous Last Words». Humans make three confident plans against Australia's rabbits, and each one backfires with a dry, ironic twist. (1) The record fence: rabbits were already on the «safe» side and were scratching to get back, yet it was still called the longest unbroken fence in the world, and its boss said there was practically nothing to fear. (2) The £25,000 prize: Louis Pasteur entered with chicken cholera, the rules protected the farm animals but forgot birds, and nobody won. (3) The quarantined virus: it escaped three years early, probably on flies, and the virus got there before the official release ceremony. It ends on one more famous last word, «Surely the next one's foolproof.» The script does not use the saturated «24 rabbits» chronology anywhere.

drafts.why_it_works:
Hook: in the first second the viewer sees a fence racing to the horizon with a rabbit question attached. The punchline («already on the other side») lands by about 7 s. It is the fresh «beaten before it was finished» angle from BRIEF.md, not the saturated «24 rabbits» opener. The script keeps one pattern throughout: a confident plan, then a deadpan twist. It suits Silas's slow villain voice, with short fragments and pauses that work as punchlines («backwards», «They forgot birds», «Nobody won», «The virus got there first»), much like episode 1's «Planned by… George Patton». Each round runs on a joke kids will get without gore. The ending is itself a new famous last word, which closes the format and tees up a sequel.

Accuracy:
- Every line maps to FACTS IDs.
- Hedges are kept: «they called it», past tense and attributed (C2); «probably on flies» (D12); «Scientists say» (D16); «was sure» paraphrases «thoroughly convinced» (C7).
- The rules line names only a subset of the protected animals, and the script never says birds were the reason Pasteur was rejected.

drafts.why_it_works: The 3-second hold comes from a sum that can't be right, «13 got on, 24 got off», spoken over a moving visual from frame 0. The hedged joke at about 7 s answers it, so the viewer gets a laugh before deciding to stay. «Round one / two / three» tells the viewer how the video is built and promises an ending, which helps hold them to the halfway point. The halfway mark (~29–31 s) lands on the biggest surprise: Louis Pasteur entering with chicken cholera. Every round ends on a short, flat punchline («scratching to get back», «Nobody ever won», «already there») and each failure is more absurd than the last: an engineering failure, then a scientific one, then the authorities losing control of their own virus. The score joke turns the story around: the flies get the only point the virus round earns, so the scoreboard stays true and Australia's zero still stands. «So far», together with the estimated 200 million, leaves the match open, which invites comments. The last line («before the ship even landed») ends on the opening frame and reads straight into «Thirteen rabbits got on a ship», which drives rewatches. Every beat comes from the fresh list in BRIEF.md. The narration measures 106 words and 662 characters (tool-counted), within the 105–120 word / 690-character budget. All hedges are kept: «family records say», «probably», «most likely», «an estimated». Nothing on the DO-NOT-SAY list is used: no «released 24», no «longest fence», no 99 %, no 10 billion, no cats or foxes. Each line has at most one label, and each label adds a date, place or source that the narration doesn't say. The big on-screen numbers (13 → 24, 1,830 km, £25,000, ≈200 million, the score) are KEYFACTs with their subtitle hidden. Every visual uses toon 3D, flat diagrams, real images from the licence-checked list, or maps. The virus is shown only as abstract glyphs, and no animal is shown sick.

The hedge becomes the first laugh at about 7 s («They probably weren't playing cards.»), which keeps the «probably» from A3 and fits Silas's dry villain voice.

Each round ends on a flat punchline: «Some were scratching to get back», «Nobody ever won», «The virus was already there». The Pasteur reveal is split into two beats («Louis Pasteur entered. With chicken cholera.»), the best comic timing of any draft.

judgments.notes:
I checked every draft line by line against FACTS.md and research/digest_facts.md. None of the drafts uses an item from the DO-NOT-SAY list, so the scores separate on hedges and framing.

A wins narrowly. It makes the most factual claims, and every number and hedge in them is right. Its weak points are small: «got there first» is vague, «kills» is in the present tense, the myxoma label says 1950 although the first trial was in 1937, and the emu wink implies something the pack doesn't say.

D is a close second and has the cleanest exact wordings: C4, D12 «most likely on flies», and the «family records say so» hedge. It loses points for its closing callback, which states the breeding at sea as fact, and for the «Australia zero» framing.

C is accurate in its details. It loses points for «Australia built a fence», which should be Western Australia and edges toward the east–west myth, and for dropping «before it was finished».

B is weakest on hedges: the 13 is unhedged in the hook, the breeding is attributed to family records, «scientists say» is dropped, and the 2015 strain appears as a human weapon.

Recommended final: A's spine with D's wording swapped in at L2 (C4 phrase), L13 (most likely on flies), L15–16 (release irony) and the D labels. Change L10 to «killed», and soften L18.

judgments.notes:
I judged one lens only: owner rules plus producibility. I counted each draft's vo_text with python. A: 114 words, 660 chars. B: 106 words, 653 chars. C: 109 words, 680 chars. D: 106 words, 661 chars. All four are inside 105–120 words and ≤ 690 chars, and all land at about 53–59 s at the ep. 1 rates (2.0 words/s, 11.5 chars/s). All four keep Atlas to exactly 3 windows using only listed acting, and none uses AI video or AI images.

C wins this lens. It has the least on-screen text, needs the fewest toon builds, handles all-ages best, has the cleanest text for TTS, and has the only honest visual for «30+ shires». Its weaknesses are a missing scoreboard, a ~5 s single-Ken-Burns beat on the attributed «longest unbroken fence» line (L5, the line to cut), and the 1888 date, which is not in FACTS.md.

Fixes that apply to every draft:
- Never shade specific WA shires. Natural Earth has no shire boundaries and FACTS does not say which shires; use abstract dots (as C does).
- Rodd Island must be toon. Natural Earth cannot resolve it.
- Do not say «Eighteen hundred thirty» (D L6). It sounds like the year 1830.
- Avoid A's double score flip in L11 and its fading 99-rabbit grid in L10.
- Keep emus to one line at most.
- Restore «Scientists say» on the 10–15-year line (B L16).
- Real photos need a credit pill that does not collide with the label. Fold the credit into the label, as B L17 and D L5 do, or move credits to the description.

synth.angle: «Australia vs Rabbits», a three-round scoreboard that loops. It is built on draft D, and the rounds now run in date order. Cold open on an impossible sum: thirteen rabbits got on a ship (family records say), twenty-four got off, and they «probably weren't playing cards». Round one, 1887: a £25,000 prize. Louis Pasteur enters with chicken cholera, the rules protected the farm animals but forgot birds, and nobody ever won. Round two, 1901–07: Western Australia's ocean-to-ocean fence. Rabbits were on the safe side before it was finished and even scratched to get back, so the fence worked backwards. Round three, 1995: a quarantined virus escapes three years early, most likely on flies. It works, and Western Australia's official release ceremony a year later finds it already there. The twist score inverts episode 1: «Rabbits two, Flies one, Australia zero.» The last line, «They were winning before the ship even landed. Probably.», dissolves back into the opening frame, so the Short loops. None of the saturated chronology is used: no «24 rabbits ruined Australia», no myxoma 99 %, no spread map, no foxes or cats, no «longest fence», no emus.

synth.vo_text:
Thirteen rabbits got on a ship, family records say.
Twenty-four got off.
They probably weren't playing cards.
Round one: a prize.
Louis Pasteur entered. With chicken cholera.
The rules protected sheep, horses, dogs. They forgot birds.
Nobody ever won.
Round two: a fence.
Before it was finished, rabbits were already on the safe side.
Some were scratching to get back.
The fence worked, backwards.
Round three: a virus, in quarantine.
It escaped three years early, most likely on flies.
And it worked.
A year later: the official release ceremony.
The virus was already there.
Score so far: Rabbits two, Flies one, Australia zero.
They were winning before the ship even landed. Probably.

synth.why_it_works:
Hook: the first 1.5 s carry an impossible sum («Thirteen rabbits got…» and then «Twenty-four got off») over toon rabbits that are already moving. The first laugh («probably weren't playing cards») lands by about 8 s, and the hedge is the joke. It avoids the saturated «24 rabbits ruined Australia» opener.

Spine: «Round one / two / three» tells the viewer how long the video is and promises a payoff. Running the rounds in date order (1887 → 1901–07 → 1995) means no «Earlier» cue is needed. The Pasteur reveal (≈12–16 s) is a second hook right where Shorts usually dip. The fence's double irony («already on the safe side», «scratching to get back», «worked, backwards») sits at the midpoint. Each round is more absurd than the last and ends on a flat Silas punchline: «They forgot birds.», «Nobody ever won.», «The fence worked, backwards.», «The virus was already there.»

Ending: «And it worked» earns the flies their point, so the «Rabbits two, Flies one, Australia zero» joke stays honest. It twists ep. 1's «Humans two. Volcano zero.» «So far» and the ≈200 million label leave the match open. The last «Probably.» calls back the hook's hedge and dissolves into the opening frame, so the Short loops.

Accuracy:
- Every line maps to FACTS IDs.
- Hedges are kept: «family records say» on the 13, «probably» on the breeding (twice), «most likely on flies», «≈ 60 %», «est.».
- The birds detail is never given as the reason Pasteur was rejected.
- The fence is framed as Western Australia, ocean to ocean.
- Nothing from DO-NOT-SAY is used.

Owner rules:
- There are 2 KEYFACTs (£25,000, the final score), each with its subtitle hidden.
- There is at most one calm label per line, and each adds a date, place, source or number the voice does not say.
- The punchline beats «cards», «birds» and «backwards» carry no text.
- Viruses are abstract glyphs, dots or a bar, the chicken is healthy, and the ceremony crate stays closed.

Production:
- Toon sets: one dock (relit for Melbourne), paddock, island hut, fence, ceremony stage, scoreboard.
- Two real photos: the Lightning lithograph and the Wardang aerial.
- Flat diagrams: shields, the fence bounce, the flies' path, the bar.
- Maps from the WA GeoJSON and Natural Earth.

Budget, tool-counted: 112 words, 686 characters, 21 sentences. The conservative formula gives 64.4 s. The brief's measured rates, which already include pauses, give 56 s (2.0 w/s) to 59.7 s (11.5 c/s).

issues.problem: This is an implied timing and cause claim that FACTS does not support. «And it worked.» with the label «≈ 60 % fewer rabbits nationwide» comes BEFORE «A year later: the official release ceremony.» The viewer therefore believes the escaped, fly-carried virus cut the national population by 60 % on its own, before any official release. The «Flies one» point then rewards that belief. D14's 60 % is the overall calicivirus result. Per digest rhd_kill it comes from Schwensow 2014, citing 1998 studies, so it covers the period after the 1996 official releases. FACTS gives no timing that puts it before the ceremony.
issues.fix: Reorder the narration to lines 15 → 17 → 18 → 16 → 19: «It escaped three years early, most likely on flies. A year later: an official release ceremony. The virus was already there. And it worked. Score so far: …». Keep the label «≈ 60 % fewer rabbits nationwide» on «And it worked.»

issues.problem: The sequence «They forgot birds.» [Atlas facepalm] → «Nobody ever won.» invites the myth in digest WAR/myths #109: that Pasteur's germ was banned because it would kill birds or wildlife. The script never gives the real main reason. FACTS D5 says the main reason for rejection (1889) was that the germ didn't spread from rabbit to rabbit. The digest calls birds only a secondary concern. «Never stated as the reason» is technically true, but the viewer is left to infer the wrong one.
issues.fix: Change the line-9 label to «Rejected 1889: the germ didn't spread rabbit to rabbit». Move «New South Wales, 1887 · nearly 1,500 entries» to line 6 («With chicken cholera.», which has no text now). A spoken alternative is «It didn't spread. Nobody won.», but that adds 13 characters and only fits with the savings listed below.

issues.problem: «three years early» is our own arithmetic on a single source. FACTS D12 says only «ahead of a release planned for 1998», and the 1998 date comes from CSIROpedia alone («due for release in 1998»). FACTS gives no month for 1998. The escape was in late September 1995, so the real gap is anywhere from about 2.3 to 3.3 years, and «three years» may overstate it.
issues.fix: «It escaped years early, most likely on flies.» (saves 6 characters). Or keep «three years early» and move the bare year to the label: «planned release: 1998 · 300+ km within weeks».

issues.problem: «the official release ceremony» uses the definite article, which implies a single national release event. FACTS D13 describes Western Australia's ceremony. The digest notes there was no single national approval date («I found no exact national approval date»), and releases happened state by state. The label fixes the place, but the spoken line still overgeneralises.
issues.fix: «A year later: an official release ceremony.» (saves 1 character; keep the label «Western Australia · 18 October 1996»).

issues.problem: «The fence worked, backwards.» implies the fence really did stop rabbits, just in the wrong direction. The only evidence is one inspection: tracks «where the rabbits were trying to scratch through to get back to the East» (C5). FACTS C10 says the fences slowed rabbits but didn't stop them. Calling the fence effective in either direction goes beyond the source, so the joke states a fact we don't have.
issues.fix: «The fence had it backwards.» (saves 1 character, same joke, and claims nothing about it working).

issues.problem: «before the ship even landed»: the digest note on A1 says «Say 'arrived', not 'released' or 'docked'». «Landed» is the docking image. PNAS also says the breeding happened «before or during» the trip and «cannot rule out interbreeding occurring after arrival». The «Probably.» hedge covers the breeding, but the verb should still follow the safe wording.
issues.fix: «They were winning before the ship even arrived. Probably.» (adds 1 character).

issues.problem: The score joke states facts. (1) The «FLIES 1» KEYFACT tile drops the «most likely» hedge from D12. (2) «Score so far … Australia zero» lets viewers believe Australia has never beaten the rabbits. That conflicts with D14, since calicivirus was Australia's own programme and cut numbers about 60 %, and with the omitted myxoma success (D7/D8). Title option 1, «Australia 0, Rabbits 2, FLIES 1», states this with no context at all.
issues.fix: Narrow the score to these rounds at no character cost: «Three rounds: Rabbits two, Flies one, Australia zero.» Prefer title option 2, «Australia vs Rabbits: 3 ROUNDS». If option 1 is used, the description should state «most likely carried by flies».

issues.problem: This is an implied claim in the visual. The ship docks at a «sunny Melbourne pier» and the crate pops open, sending a cascade of rabbits down the gangplank. On screen, that is the rabbits being RELEASED in Melbourne, and at a dock. FACTS A1 says only that 24 ARRIVED in Melbourne for Barwon Park, about 37 km from Geelong. The digest says not to say «released» or «docked», and NMA puts the release of 13 at Barwon Park.
issues.fix: Keep the crate closed on the gangplank, or let the lid lift just enough to show 24 rabbits packed inside. The crate is then carried off, with no rabbits running loose on the pier. A ship at anchor with the crate lowered by rope also avoids «docked».

issues.problem: The visual removes the hedge. The voice says «probably», but baby ears popping up in the hold show breeding at sea as fact. PNAS says «before or during» the voyage, and the TAP 2016 background offers a different explanation for 13 vs 24: 24 imported, at least 13 released.
issues.fix: Keep the deck of cards gag, but leave the hold ambiguous. For example, the crate lid jiggles and Atlas raises the magnifier with a «?», with no on-screen babies. Or have Atlas's magnifier reveal only one pair of ears.

issues.problem: The visual overstates how far construction had got. A «half-built» fence with the camera passing its end implies the fence was well advanced, perhaps half done, and that rabbits went around it. The digest note on C4 says that in 1902 «only about 50 miles of fence had been started» out of 1,139, so the rabbits were ahead of construction. The bare-red vs green split is the 1907 grass report (C8), which is anachronistic for 1902.
issues.fix: Show a short, just-started stretch of netting, then survey pegs along the planned line with no netting at all. The camera then finds the rabbit already west of the pegs. Avoid the strong red/green split until line 12 (1904) or later.

issues.problem: The visual gives flies more credit than the source does. Flies carry the virus glyphs across the strait, and their trails spread far onto the mainland under «300+ km within weeks». FACTS/digest attribute only the ESCAPE from the pens to flies: MLA found the virus on blowflies just outside the quarantine area, and CSIROpedia says «insects». FACTS gives no vector for the spread on the mainland.
issues.fix: Flies lift the glyphs out of the pens only. Show the mainland spread as a neutral dotted front advancing from the coast, with no flies on it, ending at the «300+ km within weeks» label.

issues.problem: The visual places the ceremony pin «in the middle of» the virus dots, which says the virus was already at the release site. The source (WA media statement) says it had spread through «more than 30 agricultural and southern pastoral shires in WA», and that the release was «near the Great Southern town of Cranbrook». It does not say Cranbrook was already infected.
issues.fix: Spread the abstract dots across the south-west farm belt and put the pin near Cranbrook without dots right under it. The voice «already there» means WA, and that is supported.

issues.problem: «Round one» may suggest the 1887 prize was Australia's first move against rabbits. Shooting, trapping and poison (D1), the 1883–84 mongooses (D2) and the 1886 cats (D3) all came earlier. This is framing, but it is an implied claim.
issues.fix: No VO change needed. Do not describe the prize as the «first» weapon in the description, pinned comment or titles. If space allows, the description can say «after guns, poison and mongooses…».

issues.problem: Title option 3, «Australia's £25,000 Rabbit PRIZE»: per D4 the prize was offered by the colony of New South Wales in 1887, before federation. The possessive suggests the nation of Australia offered it.
issues.fix: «A £25,000 PRIZE to Beat Australia's Rabbits».

issues.problem: Hook alternative 3, «Australia's rabbit virus escaped from a quarantine island.»: FACTS D12 says «quarantine pens on Wardang Island», not a quarantine island. «Australia's rabbit virus» can be read as Australian-made, and FACTS does not support that.

checks.notes:
I checked every number and date against FACTS.md, digest_facts.md and the research.json quotes, and they all match:
- 13 left England (family records), 24 arrived, England October 1859, Melbourne Christmas Day 1859
- £25,000, NSW 1887, nearly 1,500 entries, nobody won
- Pasteur, chicken cholera, Rodd Island; the protected animals (horses, sheep, camels, goats, swine, dogs) with birds left out
- WA fence ≈1,830 km ocean to ocean, built outward from Burracoppin (Contract 1 south, Contract 2 north)
- Rabbits on the safe side by 1902; 1904 tracks «trying to scratch through to get back to the East»
- Wardang quarantine pens 1995, escape most likely on flies, 300+ km within weeks
- ≈60 % nationwide; WA ceremony 18 Oct 1996, with 30+ WA shires already affected; ≈200 million today (est.)

No item from the DO-NOT-SAY list is used. Hedges are kept: «family records say», «probably» (×2), «most likely», «≈», «est.». The tool counts are correct: 112 words and 686 characters.

The two majors are both implied-claim problems, not wrong facts:
- The order of «And it worked» suggests the 60 % cut came before the official release.
- «They forgot birds → Nobody ever won» leaves the viewer to guess the rejection reason, and the obvious guess is the bird myth.

If all the suggested spoken fixes are taken («years early», «an official», «had it backwards», «arrived», «Three rounds:»), the narration drops to about 679 characters, which is inside the 690 limit. That leaves room for the optional «It didn't spread. Nobody won.» (+13 → about 692) only if one more cut is made.

These are well-sourced but carry some uncertainty; no change is needed:
- The 13 come from a single 1993 family memoir. TAP 2016 offers a different 13-vs-24 reading, and «family records say» covers it.
- The wording of the prize rules rests on an AAS paraphrase. The 1887 notice was not reached.
- The 1904 quote's source is dated either June or December 1904. «1904» is safe.
